activity_context.topic_title: Integration by Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Functions

feedback.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
